title: Is There a Case for Copying
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau responds to Ben Newmark's post against copying from the board by separating two practices that often get lumped together: mindless transcription and purposeful imitation of an expert. He opens with the long history of copying as a means of cultural transmission and apprenticeship, then turns sharply to the modern classroom, where copied paragraphs in exercise books frequently masquerade as evidence of learning. Drawing on the principle that we remember what we think about, he argues that board-to-book copying requires students to hold only fragments of words in working memory, so little meaningful thought occurs, and the burden falls hardest on weaker writers and spellers. The second half makes the counter-case. Using Albert Bandura's account of social learning and vicarious reinforcement, Didau argues that mimicry of worked models is a genuine bridge from novice to independent performance and offers psychological safety. Copying can also be justified in call and response, or where accuracy of a quotation, equation or definition matters. His closing test is purpose: copying is defensible only when teachers can explain how students will subsequently use what they copied, and retrieval or reconstruction is usually the better bet.
points: Didau argues that copied text in exercise books is a poor proxy for learning because students copy word groups rather than sentences, so their attention never rests on meaning.
Mindless copying compounds disadvantage: students with slow handwriting, weak spelling or tracking difficulties spend their whole attention on letter formation and keeping their place.

He distinguishes transcription from mimicry, using Bandura's model (attend to a model, remember it, be able to reproduce it, have a reason to try) to show that imitating experts is how most learning happens.
Imitation works as a scaffold only if students are then required to produce independently; otherwise they merely practise reproducing models.
Where copying is used, it should serve accuracy (quotations, equations, definitions) or oral call and response, while removing information and asking students to reconstruct it is usually superior.
quotes: Just as novice scribes learned their art by copying the work of previous generations, young artists reproduced their masters’ paintings and apprentice craftsmen imitated expert techniques. Originality was understood to emerge from long familiarity with what others had already achieved. In this way, mimicry is a stepping stone to mastery.

Once you know to look for it, students’ books are often stuffed with what is very clearly copied verbatim from something their teacher has prepared. What can look like evidence of learning all too often turns out to be evidence of a teacher’s reliance on copying as a very poor proxy.

Students don’t have to select, organise, transform or retrieve anything. All they need do is hold a few words (almost never as much as a sentence) in mind for long enough to shift their gaze from board to page. The fact that students engage word by word instead sentence by sentence means their attention isn’t on meaning.

The negative effects of mindless copying are compounded for the children who most depend on us to make progress. Those with slower, or more untidy, handwriting, weaker spelling or difficulty tracking between board and page must devote all their available attention to keeping up.

Mimicry provides a crucial bridge between being unable to perform something and being able to perform it independently. By watching a teacher construct a sentence, students can be prompted to notice the interaction between subject and verb, why a word is rejected in favour of another and how ideas change in redrafting.

Copying gives novices a map through unfamiliar terrain, temporarily carrying some of the load while their attention is directed towards the features that matter. The risk is that students practise reproducing models without getting any better at independent production. Mimicry only works as a bridge if we expect students to cross it.
If we want students to notice patterns, rehearse procedures or imitate expert performance, copying may be justified, but only if we subsequently require them to do something with what they’ve copied.

There may be occasions when accurate imitation gives novices a safe first step into more demanding expectations but if we’re going to make children copy, we should be clear about how the activity will lead to more durable learning. If we can’t give a convincing answer, we shouldn’t waste their time.
